pages.title: The Choice That Changes the View
pages.summary: Our founding message: you may not choose every circumstance, but you can learn to choose how you meet it.
pages.body:
You may not choose every circumstance. You can learn to choose how you meet it.

Life doesn't always unfold the way we hoped. We experience loss, disappointment, uncertainty, rejection, and moments when the future feels difficult to imagine.

Choosing happiness does not mean denying these experiences, forcing a smile, or blaming ourselves for feeling sad.

It means giving ourselves permission to consider another perspective.

What else might be true? What remains within my control? What can I learn? Who can help me? What is one small step I can take today?

A difficult moment can be real without defining your entire life. A setback can hurt without determining your entire future. And asking for help can be an act of strength rather than a sign of failure.

You don't have to feel happy every day to build a life with more meaning, connection, and hope.

The journey begins when you recognize that another perspective may be possible.

pages.title: About & Mission
pages.summary: Who we are, what #ChooseHappiness is for, and just as importantly what it is not.
pages.body:
## Our mission

#ChooseHappiness exists to help improve society's mental well-being and personal life perspectives through accessible education, thoughtful reflection, healthy coping practices, community, and encouragement.

## Our philosophy

> Begin the journey to choose happiness when the paths are before you.

> Happiness isn't about pretending life is perfect. It's about discovering healthier ways to meet life as it is.

## What we are

- A mental wellness **education** website with plain-language articles, guided reflections, and daily prompts.
- A **peer-support community** where people can share experiences and encourage one another.
- A place to practice small, everyday skills such as noticing thoughts, pausing, reframing, and reaching out.

## What we are not

- **Not therapy or medical care.** Nothing here is a diagnosis, treatment, or a substitute for a licensed professional.
- **Not an emergency or crisis service.** We do not monitor the site around the clock and cannot send help to you. If you are in danger or thinking about harming yourself, please see [Get Help Now](/get-help).
- **Not staffed by counselors.** Community moderators are not crisis counselors or clinicians.
- **Not a promise of outcomes.** Different things help different people, and some difficulties call for professional support.

## Who started this

#ChooseHappiness was founded by Stephen A. Parks Jr. and Gina P. McCoy, an engaged couple.

## How we approach content

- Our content is **general education**, not personal advice.
- We **cite our sources** where we make research claims, and we try to say plainly how strong the evidence is. See [Research & Evidence](/research).
- Content that touches clinically sensitive topics is intended to be **reviewed by qualified professionals** before it is presented as clinical guidance. Until that review has happened, it is clearly marked as **not yet professionally reviewed**.
- We separate established findings, emerging evidence, opinion, and brand philosophy so you can tell which is which.

pages.title: Get Help Now
pages.summary: If you are in crisis or worried about your safety, please use these services. This website is not one of them.
pages.body:
## If you are in immediate danger

**Call 911** (in the U.S.) or your local emergency number. Do not wait for a reply on this website.

## If you are thinking about suicide or are in emotional distress (U.S.)

**988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline** (free, confidential, 24/7/365)

- **Call** 988
- **Text** 988
- **Chat** online at [chat.988lifeline.org](https://chat.988lifeline.org/)
- **Veterans and service members:** dial 988, then press 1, or text 838255 (the Veterans Crisis Line). Chat is also available at [veteranscrisisline.net](https://www.veteranscrisisline.net/).
- **Spanish:** 988 text and chat are available in Spanish at [988lifeline.org/es](https://988lifeline.org/es/inicio/).
- **Deaf and hard of hearing:** ASL callers can call 988 using a videophone (VP) number. TTY users can use their preferred relay service or dial 711, then 988. Details: [988lifeline.org/deaf-hard-of-hearing-hearing-loss](https://988lifeline.org/deaf-hard-of-hearing-hearing-loss/).

## Other support (U.S.)

- **Crisis Text Line:** text **HOME** to **741741** to reach a trained volunteer Crisis Counselor, 24/7, free and confidential. Text **HOLA** to 741741 for Spanish. ([crisistextline.org](https://www.crisistextline.org/))
- **SAMHSA National Helpline:** **1-800-662-HELP (4357)**, free and confidential, 24/7, English and Spanish. It is a treatment referral and information service for mental health and substance use. ([samhsa.gov](https://www.samhsa.gov/find-help/national-helpline))
- **Find treatment near you:** [findtreatment.gov](https://findtreatment.gov/) helps you locate state-licensed mental health and substance use treatment in the U.S. and its territories.

## Outside the United States

Call your local emergency number. You can also look up a helpline for your country at [findahelpline.com](https://findahelpline.com/), a free directory run by ThroughLine. Please note that the directory is not an emergency service itself.

## What this website can and cannot do

- This site is **not monitored 24 hours a day**.
- Our moderators are **volunteers or community staff, not crisis counselors**, and not clinicians.
- We **cannot send help to your location** and we do not know where you are.
- We **do not use automated tools to predict risk** or detect who might be in crisis. If you post something worrying, no one is guaranteed to see it in time.
- Posts and messages here are **not a substitute** for contacting a crisis service or emergency responders.

## If you are worried about someone else

- If they are in immediate danger, call 911 or your local emergency number.
- If you are unsure, you can call or text 988 yourself and ask for guidance on how to support them.
- Ask directly and kindly whether they are thinking about suicide. Asking does not plant the idea. Listen without judging, and stay with them or help them connect to someone who can.
- Encourage them to contact 988, a doctor, or a mental health professional, and offer to help make the call.
- Look after yourself too. Supporting someone is hard, and you are allowed to ask for help.

*Phone numbers and services can change. We last checked these details against the official websites linked above. If a number does not work, please use the official site.*

pages.title: Research & Evidence
pages.summary: Plain-language summaries of what research suggests about five everyday practices, how strong the evidence is, and where it falls short.
pages.body:
This page summarizes research in plain language. It is education, not medical advice. Where we say a study found something, we only report numbers we read in the source itself. Effects in this field are often small to moderate, they vary between people, and these practices are not a replacement for professional care.

## How we label content

- **Established findings:** results seen repeatedly across many studies, ideally with systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Even then we say what the finding does and does not show.
- **Emerging evidence:** early or limited results, small studies, or findings that have not yet been consistently replicated.
- **Opinion:** the views of our writers or community members. Useful, but not research.
- **Brand philosophy:** our guiding beliefs, such as our manifesto. These are values, not scientific claims.

**Strength of evidence labels** used below: *Established*, *Promising*, *Emerging*, *Mixed*. These are our own plain-language judgments based on the sources listed, and they are not a formal grading. They have not yet been reviewed by a qualified professional.

---

## Social connection

**What research suggests.** A large meta-analysis of 148 studies with 308,849 participants found that people with stronger social relationships had a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up periods (odds ratio 1.50). The U.S. Surgeon General's advisory also describes links between social connection and health, including depression.

**Strength of evidence:** Established (as an association).

**Limitations.** Most of the evidence is observational, and the authors state that "causality is not easily established." Results varied a lot between studies, most measured relationships with simple measures that did not capture quality, and most data came from North America and Western Europe. Being around people does not help if the relationships are harmful.

**Sources**
- Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB. Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review. PLOS Medicine, 2010. [Link](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article/info:doi/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316)
- Office of the U.S. Surgeon General. Social Connection (advisory and fact cards). [Link](https://www.hhs.gov/surgeongeneral/reports-and-publications/connection/index.html)

---

## Mindfulness

**What research suggests.** A review of 47 trials with 3,515 participants found moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation programs improve anxiety and depression, and low evidence for stress and distress. NCCIH notes mindfulness is generally considered low risk, though about 8% of participants in studies in one review reported a negative experience.

**Strength of evidence:** Mixed.

**Limitations.** NCCIH states that "much of the research on these topics has been preliminary or not scientifically rigorous," and results "may have been interpreted too optimistically." Studies that followed people beyond about two months in one analysis found no lasting effects. Mindfulness can be uncomfortable for some people, especially those with trauma, and should not replace conventional care.

**Sources**
- Goyal M et al. Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24395196/)
- NCCIH. Meditation and Mindfulness: Effectiveness and Safety. [Link](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/meditation-and-mindfulness-what-you-need-to-know)

---

## Cognitive reappraisal (reframing)

**What research suggests.** A meta-analysis of 306 experimental comparisons found that strategies involving cognitive change, such as reappraising a situation or taking another person's perspective, had small to medium effects on emotional outcomes (overall d+ = 0.36). Attentional strategies overall showed no average effect, and suppressing thoughts of an upsetting event was slightly negative.

**Strength of evidence:** Promising.

**Limitations.** Most of the included studies were experiments that manipulated emotions for a short time, often with students or volunteers. They do not show how reframing works over months in real life, or for people with serious distress. How you reframe matters, and reframing is not about denying that something is hard.

**Sources**
- Webb TL, Miles E, Sheeran P. Dealing with feeling: a meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin, 2012. [Link](https://sussex.figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/Dealing_with_feeling_a_meta-analysis_of_the_effectiveness_of_strategies_derived_from_the_process_model_of_emotion_regulation/23396432)

---

## Gratitude practices

**What research suggests.** A meta-analysis of 27 studies with 3,675 participants found gratitude interventions had a small effect on symptoms of depression and anxiety (g = -0.29) right after the intervention.

**Strength of evidence:** Promising (small effects).

**Limitations.** The authors note that earlier reviews raised the possibility that benefits partly reflect placebo effects. The effect is small, and gratitude exercises are not a treatment for depression or anxiety. For some people, being told to "be grateful" can feel dismissive of real pain, so we encourage appreciating things without dismissing what is difficult.

**Sources**
- Cregg DR, Cheavens JS. Gratitude Interventions: Effective Self-help? A Meta-analysis of the Impact on Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety. Journal of Happiness Studies, 2021. [Link](https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/jhappi/v22y2021i1d10.1007_s10902-020-00236-6.html)

---

## Self-compassion

**What research suggests.** A meta-analysis of 27 randomized controlled trials found that self-compassion interventions were linked to moderate improvements in outcomes such as stress (g = 0.67), depression (g = 0.66), anxiety (g = 0.57), and self-criticism (g = 0.56).

**Strength of evidence:** Promising.

**Limitations.** The authors say publication bias may be present. The interventions were quite different from one another, and results varied by population. Group-delivered programs showed stronger effects than individual ones. Our summary is based on the published abstract, since the full text was not available to us.

**Sources**
- Ferrari M et al. Self-compassion interventions and psychosocial outcomes: a meta-analysis of RCTs. Mindfulness, 2019. [Link](https://acuresearchbank.acu.edu.au/item/87545/self-compassion-interventions-and-psychosocial-outcomes-a-meta-analysis-of-rcts)

---

*Research changes. If you spot an error or a newer study, please tell us so we can update this page.*

## 1. Who we are

#ChooseHappiness ("we," "us") is a mental wellness education and peer-support website operated by its founders, Stephen A. Parks Jr. and Gina P. McCoy. Contact: [owner email address].

This is not a health care provider. We are **not a HIPAA covered entity**, and we do not claim HIPAA compliance or any security certification.

## 2. Information we collect

- **Account information:** email address, display name, and password (stored in hashed form by our authentication provider).
- **Content you create:** private journal entries, community posts and replies, chat messages, and any files you upload.
- **Reports and moderation records:** reports you submit and actions taken on content or accounts.
- **Basic technical data** needed to run the service, such as session information.

## 3. Where your data is stored

We use **Supabase** to provide authentication, a Postgres database, file storage, and realtime features. Your data is hosted with Supabase and its infrastructure providers under their terms.

## 4. Private journal entries

- Journal entries are protected by **row-level security** so that only **you** can read your own entries through the app.
- **Administrators and moderators cannot read your journal entries through the app.**
- However, people with **database-level or infrastructure access** could technically read stored data. This includes our hosting provider and the owners' project administrators who hold service credentials. We do not intend to access journal entries, and we [describe internal access policy here].
- We may **disclose information if legally required**, such as in response to valid legal process.
- Journal entries are not end-to-end encrypted.

## 5. Community content, reports, and messages

Community posts are visible to other members according to the settings of each space. When you **report** a post or message, it becomes visible to moderators so they can review it. Chat messages are kept for [X days], then deleted.

## 6. What we do not do

- We do **not** show advertising.
- We do **not** sell your personal data.
- We do **not** use third-party tracking or analytics by default. If we add analytics in the future, we will update this policy, and we will not send sensitive content (such as journal text or messages) to analytics tools.
- We do **not** use automated tools to predict or monitor your risk.

## 7. Email

We send **transactional emails only**, such as sign-in links, password resets, and account notices. We do not send marketing email unless you opt in.

## 8. Your choices

In **Account settings** you can **export your data** and **delete your account**.

## 9. Retention

When you delete content or your account, the content is removed from our active systems. [Describe any backup retention period.] Chat message retention is set by the owners at [X days]. Moderation records may be kept for [period] to enforce our rules.

## 10. Security

We use reasonable technical measures, including access controls, but no system is perfectly secure and we cannot guarantee absolute security.

## 11. Children and teens

Member accounts are for **adults 18 and older**. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18; if we learn that we have, we will delete it. Visitors under 18 can still read the public educational pages without an account. *[Legal review needed: COPPA, state minor-privacy laws, and whether to allow teen accounts in the future.]*

## 12. Emergencies

We do not monitor accounts for emergencies. If you are in crisis, see [Get Help Now](/get-help).

## 13. Changes to this policy

We will post changes here and update the date above. [Describe notice for material changes.]

## 14. Contact

[Owner email address]

pages.title: Community Guidelines
pages.summary: How we treat each other here, what moderators do and do not do, and what happens when rules are broken.
pages.body:
#ChooseHappiness is a space for encouragement and shared experience. These guidelines help it stay kind and safe.

## How we show up

- **Be kind.** Assume good intent, listen, and disagree gently.
- **Share experiences, not diagnoses or medical advice.** Say "this helped me" instead of "you have..." or "you should stop taking...". Do not tell others to start or stop medication or treatment.
- **Do not promote self-harm, suicide, or methods.** No details about methods, and no encouragement of harming oneself or others. If you are struggling, please see [Get Help Now](/get-help).
- **Use content warnings** for heavy topics such as loss, violence, abuse, or self-harm, so people can choose whether to read.
- **Protect privacy.** Do not share other people's personal information, private messages, or identifying details. Be careful with your own.
- **No harassment or hate.** No bullying, threats, slurs, or attacks based on race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, or other identity.
- **No spam or selling.** No advertising, solicitation, or promoting products and services.

## Peer support is not professional care

Members are not therapists, and you should not treat what you read as professional advice. Support from peers can be valuable alongside professional help, not instead of it.

## How reporting works

Use the **Report** button on any post or message. A report makes that content visible to moderators, who review it against these guidelines. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, do not rely on a report. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

## What moderators do and do not do

**Moderators do:** review reported content, remove content that breaks the guidelines, send warnings, and suspend or ban accounts when needed.

**Moderators do not:** provide counseling or crisis support, diagnose, give medical advice, read private journal entries through the app, or watch the site around the clock. Unless the owners say otherwise on this page, moderation is **not 24/7**, and review may take time.

## Consequences

Depending on the situation, we may take these steps:

1. Content removal
2. Warning
3. Suspension
4. Ban

Serious violations, such as threats or encouraging self-harm, may lead to immediate suspension or ban.

## Appeals

If you think we made a mistake, you can appeal by contacting [owner email address] and explaining what happened. We will review it in good faith.

journeys.title: A moment of calm when you feel overwhelmed
journeys.summary: A short guided pause to slow down, name what is happening, and choose one small next step.

steps.title: Pause and notice
steps.body: Stop what you can for a minute. Put both feet on the floor and **breathe out slowly**, longer than you breathe in. Do this a few times.

steps.title: Name what you feel
steps.body: Try to put a word on it: *stressed, scared, angry, sad, tired.* Naming a feeling is not the same as agreeing with it.
steps.reflect_prompt: What am I feeling right now, and where do I feel it in my body?

steps.title: Learn about stress
steps.body: Stress is a normal response, and it can feel intense. Read a short piece on what stress is and what can help.

steps.title: Sort what you can influence
steps.body: Make two short lists: things you **can** influence today, and things you **cannot**. Circle one thing from the first list.
steps.reflect_prompt: What is one thing I can influence today?

steps.title: Choose one small step
steps.body: Pick one small action for the next hour, such as water, a walk, a message to someone, or a task you can finish in five minutes. If you feel unsafe, please see **Get Help Now**.
steps.reflect_prompt: What small action would support my well-being today?

journeys.title: Untangling a thought
journeys.summary: Slow down a stressful thought, separate facts from assumptions, and look for another possible view.

steps.title: Write the thought down
steps.body: Write the thought exactly as it shows up, like *"I always mess things up."* Seeing it on the screen can give it some distance.
steps.reflect_prompt: What is the thought I keep returning to?

steps.title: Separate facts from assumptions
steps.body: Which parts could a neutral observer confirm? Which parts are a guess, a prediction, or a feeling presented as a fact?

steps.title: Ask what else might be true
steps.body: Look for at least one other explanation, even if it feels less likely right now. You do not have to believe it yet.
steps.reflect_prompt: What else might be true? What would I say to a friend in my situation?

steps.title: Be gentle with yourself
steps.body: Notice the tone of your inner voice. Try saying something to yourself that you would say to someone you care about.

steps.title: Decide on a next step
steps.body: Is there one small thing you can do, check, or ask? Write it down.
steps.reflect_prompt: What is one small step I can take today?

journeys.title: Reconnecting with someone
journeys.summary: A gentle path from thinking about someone to sending a simple message.

steps.title: Think of one person
steps.body: Think of someone you have drifted from, or someone who has been kind to you. It does not have to be a big relationship.
steps.reflect_prompt: Who comes to mind when I think of someone I would like to hear from?

steps.title: Notice what gets in the way
steps.body: Worries like *"they are too busy"* or *"it will be awkward"* are common. Are they facts, or assumptions?

steps.title: Start with appreciation
steps.body: What do you appreciate about this person? Gratitude can make a message feel easier to write and warmer to receive.
steps.reflect_prompt: What is one thing I appreciate about them?

steps.title: Reach out
steps.body: Send a short, low-pressure message, such as *"Hey, I was thinking about you. How have you been?"* A reply is not required for it to be worth sending.

steps.title: Plan a follow-up
steps.body: If it goes well, pick a small next step, like a call or coffee. If you do not hear back, that is not a verdict on you or the relationship.
